text: A or an depends on the SOUND, not the letter: “an hour” (silent h), “a university” (starts with /j/), “an MBA”.
First mention takes “a”, the next one takes “the”: “I saw a dog. The dog was huge.”
No article when talking in general about plural or uncountable nouns: “I like music”, “Dogs are loyal”.
No article with meals, languages and most countries: “I have breakfast”, “She speaks Polish”, “I live in Poland”. But: “the Netherlands”, “the USA”.
Sports take no article, instruments take “the”: “play football”, but “play the guitar”.
“the” goes with unique things: “the sun”, “the sky”, “the internet”, and with superlatives: “the best”, “the most expensive”.
“go to school / work / bed” has no “the” when you mean the activity: “I go to work by bus”. Use “the” for the building: “I went to the school to meet a teacher”.
Present Perfect when the result matters now, Past Simple with a finished time: “I’ve lost my keys” vs “I lost my keys yesterday”. Never “I have seen him yesterday”.
for + a period, since + a starting point: “for three years”, “since 2020”, “since Monday”.
Present Simple for habits and timetables (“The train leaves at 6”). Present Continuous for now and fixed plans: “I’m meeting Anna tomorrow”.
State verbs usually have no -ing form: “I know”, “I understand”, “I want”, “I believe”, not “I am knowing”.
After when / if / as soon as / before / until, use the present for the future: “I’ll call you when I arrive”, not “when I will arrive”.
Past Continuous sets the scene, Past Simple gives the event: “I was cooking when she called”.
“used to + verb” is a past habit: “I used to smoke”. “be used to + -ing” means being accustomed: “I’m used to getting up early”.
“will” for decisions made at the moment of speaking (“I’ll help you”), “be going to” for plans and visible evidence: “I’m going to study law”, “Look at those clouds, it’s going to rain”.
Past Perfect shows the earlier of two past actions: “When I arrived, the film had already started”.
“has been to Paris” = went and came back; “has gone to Paris” = went and is still there.
Frequency adverbs go before the main verb but after “be”: “She always drinks tea”, “She is always late”.
Usual order: manner → place → time: “She sang beautifully at the party last night”.
In questions the auxiliary comes before the subject: “Where do you live?”. In embedded questions the order goes back to normal: “Do you know where he lives?”.
Don’t put an adverb between the verb and its object: “I like football very much”, not “I like very much football”.
Adjectives go before the noun and never take a plural: “two red cars”. Order: opinion, size, age, colour, material: “a beautiful old wooden table”.
An English sentence needs a subject: “It’s raining”, “There is a problem”. Polish “Pada” and “Jest problem” don’t work without “it” and “there”.
One negative per clause: “I don’t know anything” or “I know nothing”, not “I don’t know nothing”.
Time: “at” for clock times and points (at 5, at night), “on” for days and dates (on Monday, on 5 May), “in” for months, years and parts of the day (in May, in 2026, in the morning).
No preposition after these verbs: “discuss something”, “marry someone”, “enter a room”, “mention something”, “answer a question”.
“arrive in” a city or country, “arrive at” a specific place: “arrive in Warsaw”, “arrive at the station”.
Fixed pairs: “good at”, “interested in”, “afraid of”, “depend on”, “listen to”, “wait for”, “look at”, “different from”.
After a preposition the verb takes -ing: “interested in learning”, “good at cooking”, “before leaving”.
Uncountable in English: advice, information, news, furniture, luggage, equipment, money. No “-s” and no “a”: “some advice”, “a piece of advice”, never “informations”.
“many” with countable nouns (many friends), “much” with uncountable ones (much time). In positive sentences “a lot of” is more natural: “I have a lot of time”.
“a few” = some (positive), “few” = hardly any; “a little” = some, “little” = hardly any: “I have a few friends” vs “I have few friends”.
“fewer” with countable nouns, “less” with uncountable ones: “fewer people”, “less water”.
Age: “I am 25 years old”, not “I have 25 years”. Likewise: “I am cold / hungry / right”.
“People” is plural: “People are friendly”, not “People is”.
“agree” is a verb: “I agree”, not “I am agree”.
“make” vs “do”: make a decision / a mistake / a meal; do homework / the dishes / business. “Make a photo” should be “take a photo”.
“say” vs “tell”: “She told me that…”, “She said that…” or “She said to me”. Never “She said me”.
“borrow” = take from someone, “lend” = give to someone: “Can I borrow your pen?”, “Can you lend me your pen?”.
“learn” = gain knowledge, “teach” = help someone learn: “I learn English”, “She teaches me English”.
“explain” and “suggest” don’t take “me” directly: “explain it to me”, “suggest that I go”, not “explain me”.
“bring” = carry towards here, “take” = carry away from here: “Bring it here”, “Take it to the kitchen”.
You “steal” things but “rob” places and people: “steal a wallet”, “rob a bank”.
You “win” a game or prize but “beat” a person or team: “win the match”, “beat Germany”.
“who” for people, “which” for things, “that” for both in defining clauses: “the man who called”, “the book that I read”.
“remember to do” = not forget a task; “remember doing” = recall a past action: “Remember to lock the door” vs “I remember locking it”.
“enjoy”, “avoid”, “suggest”, “finish” take -ing; “want”, “decide”, “hope” take to + verb: “I enjoy swimming”, “I want to swim”.
“look forward to” is followed by -ing because “to” is a preposition here: “I look forward to seeing you”.
First conditional: if + Present, will: “If it rains, we’ll stay home”. No “will” after “if”.
Second conditional: if + Past, would: “If I had more time, I would learn Spanish”. Use “were” for all persons: “If I were you…”.
Third conditional (the past): if + Past Perfect, would have + past participle: “If I had known, I would have called”.
“unless” = “if not”: “Unless you hurry, you’ll be late”. Don’t add another “not” after “unless”.
No “to” and no “-s” after modal verbs: “She can swim”, “He must go”. Never “She can to swim” or “He cans”.
“mustn’t” is a prohibition (“You mustn’t smoke here”), “don’t have to” means no obligation (“You don’t have to come”).
“should have + past participle” expresses regret or criticism about the past: “You should have called me”.
Be polite: “Could you…?” and “I’d like…” sound better than “Can you…?” and “I want…”.
“actual” means real, not Polish “aktualny” (that’s “current”). “actually” = in fact.
“eventually” means in the end, not Polish “ewentualnie” (that’s “possibly” or “alternatively”).
“sympathetic” means feeling pity for someone, not Polish “sympatyczny” (that’s “nice” or “friendly”).
“fabric” is cloth, not a “fabryka” (that’s “factory”). “magazine” is a periodical, not a “magazyn” (that’s “warehouse”).
“preservative” is a food additive, not “prezerwatywa”. “physician” is a doctor, not a “fizyk” (that’s “physicist”).
“chef” is a head cook, your workplace “szef” is a “boss” or “manager”. “ordinary” means normal, not “ordynarny” (that’s “vulgar”).
“sensible” = reasonable, “sensitive” = easily hurt or upset. “pretend” means to act as if, not “pretendować”.
“evidence” means proof, not “ewidencja” (that’s “records”). “pension” is a retirement income, not a “pensjonat” (that’s “guesthouse”).
“give up” = stop trying or quit, “find out” = discover, “look up” = check in a dictionary, “run out of” = have none left.
Separable: “turn the light off” and “turn it off”. A pronoun goes in the middle, never “turn off it”.
“put off” = postpone, “carry on” = continue, “get along with” = have a good relationship with, “take off” = leave the ground (a plane) or remove.
“take a shower / a break / a risk / a photo”, “have a look / a meal / a rest”: these nouns go with “take” or “have”, not “make”.
Natural pairs: “heavy rain”, “strong coffee”, “fast food”, “keep a secret”, “break a promise”, “pay attention”, “catch a cold”.
“make progress”, “make an effort”, “make money”, “do research”, “do your best”, “do someone a favour”.
Tag questions: a positive statement gets a negative tag and the other way round: “You like tea, don’t you?”, “She isn’t here, is she?”.
Comparatives take “than”, never “then”: “bigger than”. Long adjectives use “more”: “more beautiful”. Pattern “the more… the better”: “The more you practise, the better you get”.
After “one of the”, the noun is plural but the verb is singular: “One of my friends lives in Berlin”.
“too” = more than needed; “enough” goes AFTER an adjective but BEFORE a noun: “too cold to swim”, “good enough”, “enough time”.
Reported speech shifts the tense back: “I am tired” → “She said she was tired”; “I will come” → “He said he would come”.
Passive voice: be + past participle: “The book was written in 1990”, “English is spoken here”.
When an action is the subject of a sentence, use -ing: “Swimming is fun”, “Learning takes time”.
Possessive ’s: “Anna’s book”, “my parents’ house”. Plurals take NO apostrophe: “the 1990s”, “two dogs”.
“it’s” = it is or it has; “its” = belonging to it: “The dog wagged its tail. It’s happy”.
After a number, “hundred / thousand / million” take no -s: “three thousand people”. With -s only in general: “thousands of people”.
Capital letters for days, months, languages and nationalities: “Monday”, “July”, “Polish”, “English”. And always “I”.
The -ed ending has three sounds: /t/ (worked), /d/ (played), /ɪd/ (wanted, needed). /ɪd/ only after t and d.
Stress moves within word families: “PHOtograph” but “phoTOGraphy”.
Silent letters: “knife”, “hour”, “Wednesday”, “island”, “castle”, “psychology”.
The “th” sounds: /θ/ in “think”, “three” (tongue between the teeth, no voice) and /ð/ in “this”, “mother” (same, but voiced).
Rivers, seas, oceans and mountain ranges take “the”: “the Vistula”, “the Baltic Sea”, “the Alps”. No “the” for lakes and single mountains: “Lake Geneva”, “Mount Everest”.
A job after “be” needs “a / an”: “She is a doctor”, “He is an engineer”.
Frequency uses “a” for “per”: “once a week”, “twice a day”, “three times a year”.
“What a…!” and “such a…” go with singular countable nouns: “What a beautiful day!”, “such a mess”. Plurals drop “a”: “such beautiful days”.
“the” + adjective means a group of people: “the rich”, “the young”, “the unemployed”.
Always with “the”: “the same”, “the next”, “the other”, “the only”: “the same problem”, “the next day”.
Fixed phrases without an article: “at home”, “in bed”, “by car”, “on foot”, “for lunch”, “at night”.
Public places usually take “the”: “the cinema”, “the bank”, “the supermarket”: “I’m going to the cinema”.
Universities: “the University of Warsaw”, but “Warsaw University”. When there’s an “of”, there’s a “the”.
“a hundred”, “a thousand”, “a quarter”, “a half”: here “a” replaces “one”.
“just”, “already”, “yet” with Present Perfect: “I’ve just finished”, “She has already left”, “Have you finished yet?”. “yet” only in questions and negatives.
“ever” in questions, “never” in answers: “Have you ever been to London?”, “I’ve never tried sushi”.
“ago” needs Past Simple: “I moved here two years ago”. “for” goes with Present Perfect: “I’ve lived here for two years”.
“How long…?” about something lasting until now: “How long have you lived here?”, not “How long do you live here?”.
Present Perfect Continuous: an action in progress or with a visible result: “I’ve been waiting for an hour”, “Your eyes are red. Have you been crying?”.
“will” also for predictions and opinions: “I think she’ll pass the exam”, “It will probably rain”.
“when” for something certain, “if” for something possible: “When I’m 30, I’ll buy a house”, “If I get the job, I’ll move”.
Past Simple questions and negatives use “did” + the base verb: “Did you see him?”, never “Did you saw him?”.
Learn the three forms of irregular verbs: go – went – gone, see – saw – seen, write – wrote – written, buy – bought – bought.
“would” for past habits: “When I was a child, we would visit grandma every Sunday”. Not for states: not “I would live there”.
“not… anymore” = no longer: “I don’t live there anymore”. “still” = continuing: “She still lives there”.
Future Continuous: “This time tomorrow I’ll be flying to Rome”: something will be in progress at that time.
Imperatives: “Don’t be late!”, “Be quiet”. “Let’s” = shall we: “Let’s go”, negative “Let’s not argue”.
“There is” + singular, “there are” + plural: “There is a book”, “There are two books”. The verb agrees with the first noun after “there”.
Questions with “who / what” as the subject take no “do”: “Who called you?”. As the object they do: “Who did you call?”.
Two objects: “give me the book” or “give the book to me”. With “to” the order flips.
“also” goes before the main verb: “She also speaks French”. After “be”: “He is also tired”.
“Yesterday” can open or close a sentence: “Yesterday I met Tom” or “I met Tom yesterday”.
An “if” clause at the start takes a comma: “If you come, I’ll help”. At the end, no comma: “I’ll help if you come”.
Inversion after negative adverbs: “Never have I seen such a mess”, “Rarely do we eat out”.
“So do I” and “Neither do I”: “I like tea.” — “So do I.”, “I don’t like coffee.” — “Neither do I.”.
Unlike Polish “że”, English usually has no comma before “that”: “I think that it’s true”.
“in time” = early enough; “on time” = exactly as scheduled: “The train arrived on time”.
“at the end of” = the last part of something specific; “in the end” = finally: “In the end, we won”.
“by” = no later than, “until” = up to that moment: “Finish it by Friday”, “I’ll wait until Friday”.
“during” + noun, “while” + clause: “during the lesson”, “while I was sleeping”.
“between” for two (or clearly separate things), “among” for many: “between you and me”, “among friends”.
Place: “at the bus stop”, “on the table”, “in the box”, “on the second floor”. Transport: “in a car”, “on a bus”.
“angry with” a person, “angry about” a thing: “angry with him”, “angry about the delay”.
“famous for” (the reason), “known as” (the role or name): “famous for its beaches”, “known as the best”.
“look for” = search, “look after” = take care of, “look at” = direct your eyes, “look forward to” = anticipate happily.
“think of” for opinions (“What do you think of it?”), “think about” for considering (“I’m thinking about moving”).
“spend money on”, “spend time + -ing”: “I spent two hours reading”.
“on the phone”, “on TV”, “on the radio”, “by email”, “in the newspaper”.
“at Christmas” in general, “on Christmas Day” for that one day.
“ask for”, “apply for”, “search for”, “pay for”: “pay for the meal”. But “pay the bill”, without “for”.
“married to” (not “with”): “She is married to a pilot”. “Divorced from”, or just “divorced”.
“on the left”, “on the right”, but “in the middle”, “in the corner”, “at the top / bottom”.
Count uncountables with units: “a glass of water”, “a slice of bread”, “two pieces of furniture”.
“hair” as in all the hair on your head is uncountable: “Her hair is long”. “a hair” is a single strand.
“work” (in general) is uncountable, “job” is countable: “I have a lot of work”, “I found a new job”.
“travel” is uncountable, “trip” is countable: “Travel is fun”, “a business trip”.
“weather”, “knowledge”, “progress”, “research” are uncountable: “The weather is nice”, “You’re making progress”.
“police” is plural: “The police are here”. “news” is singular: “The news is good”.
-ed describes a feeling, -ing the cause: “I’m bored”, “It’s boring”; “I’m interested”, “It’s interesting”.
“tell a lie / the truth / a joke / a story”, but “say hello / goodbye / thank you”.
After “make” and “let”, use the bare infinitive: “She made me laugh”, “Let me go”.
“home” takes no “to”: “I’m going home”, not “I’m going to home”. But “go to the house”.
“Everybody”, “everyone”, “somebody”, “nobody” take a singular verb: “Everybody is here”.
Only one “s” in the 3rd person: “He doesn’t know” (not “doesn’t knows”), “Does she work?” (not “Does she works?”).
Polish “swój” becomes “my / your / his / her / our / their” depending on the owner: “He took his book”, “She took her book”.
“good” is an adjective, “well” is an adverb: “a good speaker”, “She speaks English well”.
“hard” = with effort, “hardly” = almost not: “He works hard”, “I can hardly see”. “late” = not on time, “lately” = recently.
“quite” = fairly, “quiet” = silent: “It’s quite cold”, “Be quiet”.
“lose” /luːz/ = no longer have, “loose” /luːs/ = not tight: “Don’t lose your keys”, “loose trousers”.
“affect” (verb) = influence, “effect” (noun) = result: “The weather affects my mood”, “a side effect”.
“advice” (noun) and “advise” (verb): “Let me give you some advice”, “I advise you to go”.
“alone” = without company (a fact), “lonely” = sad about it (a feeling): “She lives alone but isn’t lonely”.
“beside” = next to, “besides” = also or in addition: “sit beside me”, “Besides, it’s late”.
“rise” takes no object (“Prices rise”), “raise” takes one (“They raise prices”).
“fun” = enjoyment, “funny” = makes you laugh: “The party was fun”, “a funny joke”.
No preposition: “visit Rome”, “meet someone”, “reach the top”, “call someone” (not “call to”).
“try doing” = test something out (“try adding salt”); “try to do” = make an effort (“try to open the door”).
“stop doing” = quit, “stop to do” = pause in order to do: “stop smoking” vs “stop to smoke”.
Purpose takes “to” + verb: “I went to the shop to buy milk”, not “for buy milk”.
“maybe” (adverb) vs “may be” (verb): “Maybe it’s true”, “It may be true”.
“everyday” (adjective) vs “every day” (adverb): “everyday life”, “I run every day”.
“a lot” is two words: “a lot of time”, never “alot”.
“in case” = as a precaution: “Take an umbrella in case it rains”, not “in case of it rains”.
“like” = similar to, “as” = in the role of: “He works as a teacher”, “He swims like a fish”.
Zero conditional: if + Present, Present: facts and general truths. “If you heat ice, it melts”.
“wish” + Past Simple is about the present: “I wish I had a car”. + Past Perfect is about the past: “I wish I had known”.
“would rather” + base verb: “I’d rather stay home”. “had better” works the same: “You’d better hurry”.
“as long as” and “provided that” = only if: “You can go as long as you’re back by ten”.
Mixed conditional: “If I had studied, I would have a better job now”: past condition, present result.
“can” has no infinitive or future: “I will be able to help”, not “I will can”.
“might” ≈ “may” for possibility: “It might rain”. “could” works too: “She could be late”.
“have to” takes “do” in questions and negatives: “Do I have to go?”, “You don’t have to come”.
“ought to” ≈ “should”: “You ought to see a doctor”.
“must” only works in the present; for the past use “had to”: “I had to leave early”.
“be allowed to” = have permission: “We’re not allowed to park here”.
“needn’t” and “don’t need to” = not necessary: “You needn’t come” / “You don’t need to come”.
“Would you mind + -ing?” asks a favour: “Would you mind opening the window?”.
“complexion” is the colour and texture of your skin, not a “kompleks” (that’s “complex” or “inferiority complex”).
“dress” is a garment or to put on clothes; Polish “ubranie” is “clothes”: “a nice dress”, “put on clothes”.
“prospect” means a possibility or outlook, not “prospekt” (that’s “leaflet” or “brochure”).
“lecture” is a university talk, not a “lektura” (that’s “reading” or “set text”).
“recipe” is for cooking, “prescription” is from a doctor (Polish “recepta”).
“professor” is a university academic; a school teacher is a “teacher”.
“hazard” means danger, not Polish “hazard” (that’s “gambling”): “a fire hazard”.
“terrific” means excellent, not “straszny” (that’s “terrible” or “terrifying”).
“gymnasium” is a sports hall, not a “gimnazjum” (that’s “lower secondary school”).
“novel” is a long book, not a “nowela” (that’s “short story”).
“career” is a profession path, “carrier” transports things. Polish “staż” is “internship”, not “stage”.
“cabinet” is a cupboard (or a government, “the cabinet”), not a “kabina” (that’s “cabin” or “booth”).
“get up” = leave your bed, “wake up” = stop sleeping, “sit down”, “stand up”.
“pick up” = lift or collect, “drop off” = leave someone or something somewhere, “set off” = start a journey.
“break down” = stop working (a car), “break up” = end a relationship, “break in” = enter by force.
“come across” = find by chance, “come up with” = think of, “come back” = return.
“check in” = register on arrival, “check out” = leave a hotel or examine something.
“hang out” = spend time, “hang up” = end a phone call, “call off” = cancel.
“bring up” = raise a child (or mention a topic), “grow up” = become an adult, “take care of” = look after.
“work out” = exercise or solve, “figure out” = understand, “point out” = draw attention to.
“fill in a form” = complete it, “sign up” = register, “log in” = enter an account.
“turn up” = arrive or increase the volume, “turn down” = lower the volume or reject an offer.
“catch up with” = reach someone ahead, “keep up with” = stay at the same level, “get over” = recover from.
“run into” = meet by chance, “run away” = flee, “end up” = finally become or be somewhere.
“turn out” = prove to be, “throw away” = put in the bin, “cut down” = reduce.
Inseparable: “look after the kids” → “look after them”, never “look them after”.
“show off” = display proudly, “give back” = return, “make up” = invent or reconcile.
“make a call / a plan / a noise / a difference / friends”, “make a living” = earn money to live.
“take an exam” = sit it, “pass” = succeed, “fail” = not succeed.
“pay a visit”, “pay a bill”, “pay attention”: “pay” forms several fixed phrases.
“run a business”, “run a marathon”, “run late” (be behind schedule).
“catch a bus / a cold / a ball”, but “miss a bus”: “I missed the last train”.
“save time / money”, “waste time”, “spend time”: “Don’t waste your time”.
“give a speech / an answer / permission / a hand” (help).
“keep in touch”, “keep calm”, “keep quiet”, “keep a promise”.
“do the shopping”, “do the laundry”, “do the cooking”, “do business”.
“heavy traffic”, “strong wind”, “heavy smoker”, “strong accent”: each adjective fits only certain nouns.
“take place” = happen, “take part in” = participate, “take advantage of” = make use of.
“go swimming / shopping / running / skiing”: “go” + -ing for activities.
“whose” shows possession: “the man whose car was stolen”.
After a comma, “which” refers to the whole sentence: “He passed, which surprised us”.
In defining clauses you can drop “that / who” when it is the object: “the book (that) I read”.
“have something done” = arrange for someone else to do it: “I had my hair cut”, “She’s having the car repaired”.
Use “myself” when subject and object are the same: “I cut myself”. But: “I feel good” (no “myself”).
“each other” = one another: “They love each other”.
“so” + adjective, “such” + (adjective +) noun: “so big”, “such a big house”.
“either… or” and “neither… nor”: “Either you leave or I do”, “Neither he nor she knew”.
“both… and” and “not only… but also”: “both cheap and good”.
“every” + singular, “all” + plural: “Every student has a book”, “All students have books”.
“some” in positive sentences and offers, “any” in questions and negatives: “Would you like some tea?”, “I don’t have any”.
“someone”, “anyone”, “no one” take a singular verb: “Someone is waiting”.
Short adjectives: “taller”, “happier” (y→ier), “bigger” (doubling). Irregular: good – better – best, bad – worse – worst.
“as… as”: “as tall as”, “not as old as”, “the same as”.
Tag for “I am”: “I’m late, aren’t I?”: yes, “aren’t”.
“It takes + time + to…”: “It takes me an hour to get there”.
Reported questions: “She asked where I lived”: normal word order, no “do”.
Reported commands: “He told me to sit down”.
“comfortable” is usually /ˈkʌmftəbl/: 3 syllables, the middle “or” disappears.
-ough has many sounds: “through” /θruː/, “though” /ðəʊ/, “thought” /θɔːt/, “tough” /tʌf/, “cough” /kɒf/.
The ending -s: /s/ (cats), /z/ (dogs), /ɪz/ after s, z, sh, ch (buses).
“read” is /riːd/ in the present and /red/ in the past.
Stress separates parts of speech: “REcord” (noun), “reCORD” (verb); “PREsent” vs “preSENT”.
“schedule”: BrE /ˈʃedjuːl/, AmE /ˈskedʒuːl/.
The schwa /ə/ is the most common English sound: “about”, “banana”, “teacher”: unstressed syllables are weak.
“ship” /ɪ/ (short) vs “sheep” /iː/ (long): vowel length changes the word.
“however” = but; it takes a comma after it: “It was cold. However, we went out.”.
“although” + clause, “despite / in spite of” + noun or -ing: “Although it rained…”, “Despite the rain…”.
“because” + clause, “because of” + noun: “because it rained”, “because of the rain”.
“Excuse me” before asking or interrupting, “sorry” after a mistake.
“your” = belonging to you, “you’re” = you are. “there” = that place, “their” = belonging to them, “they’re” = they are.
BrE vs AmE: “colour / color”, “centre / center”, “realise / realize”, “favourite / favorite”.
“i” before “e” except after “c”: “believe”, “receive”. Exceptions: “weird”, “science”.
Double the consonant after a short vowel: “stop → stopped”, “run → running”.
“study → studies”, but “play → plays”: consonant + y → “ies”.
“knife → knives”, “leaf → leaves”, “wife → wives”: f / fe → ves.
Irregular plurals: man – men, child – children, foot – feet, tooth – teeth, person – people, mouse – mice.
6:30 = “half past six”, 6:15 = “a quarter past six”, 6:45 = “a quarter to seven”.
Dates: “5 May” is read “the fifth of May”; in AmE “May 5th” is “May fifth”.
Years: 1999 = “nineteen ninety-nine”, 2026 = “twenty twenty-six”, 2005 = “two thousand (and) five”.
“billion” is 1,000,000,000 (Polish “miliard”), not “bilion”. “trillion” is 10^12 (Polish “bilion”).
Zero: “zero” (in general), “oh” (in numbers), “nil” (in football scores).
Decimals use a point: 3.5 is read “three point five”.
“a piece of cake” = very easy (Polish: bułka z masłem): “The exam was a piece of cake”.
“break a leg” = good luck (Polish: połamania nóg).
“It’s raining cats and dogs” = it’s pouring (Polish: leje jak z cebra).
“once in a blue moon” = very rarely (Polish: od wielkiego dzwonu).
“hit the nail on the head” = say exactly the right thing (Polish: trafić w sedno).
“under the weather” = feeling a bit ill.
“spill the beans” = reveal a secret.
“the ball is in your court” = it’s your turn to act.
“cost an arm and a leg” = be very expensive (Polish: kosztować majątek).
“bite the bullet” = face something unpleasant bravely.
“kill two birds with one stone” = solve two problems at once (Polish: upiec dwie pieczenie przy jednym ogniu).
“when pigs fly” = never (Polish: jak świnie zaczną latać).
